opening.text: Every parent knows the voice from the back seat on a long drive. “Are we there yet?” The trip is not over, and it feels like it never will be. Nobody wants to be in the car forever. But the only way to reach the place is to keep driving.
Life has long drives in it. We want the blessing now, and the road is still going. Let us look at what patience really means for those who are on the road.

mainMessage.text: Patience is not sitting in the parked car. It is driving, one mile at a time, with trust in where we are going. The Lord is with us on the road, and the road changes us.

blocks.text: **Driving is not the same as sitting.** A driver on a long trip is not idle. Hands are on the wheel and eyes are on the road. Waiting with faith is active too. We pray, serve and keep the commandments while we wait.

Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain. Be ye also patient; stablish your hearts: for the coming of the Lord draweth nigh.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, Second Counselor in the First Presidency, said this in his talk “Continue in Patience” from the April 2010 general conference (Priesthood Session).
Patience means active waiting and enduring.
We keep our hands on the wheel.

**Enjoy the road, do not just survive it.** A family can sit in silence and count the miles. Or they can sing, talk and look out the window. How we travel matters. We can wait with gratitude and kindness, even when the trip is long.
But that ye have patience, and bear with those afflictions, with a firm hope that ye shall one day rest from all your afflictions.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, Second Counselor in the First Presidency, said this in his talk “Continue in Patience” from the April 2010 general conference (Priesthood Session).
Patience is not simply enduring; it is enduring well!
How we wait is part of the journey.

**Every mile builds the driver.** Long drives make people steadier and calmer. In the same way, patience shapes us. The things we are waiting for are not the only thing that matters. Who we are becoming matters too.
And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope:
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, Second Counselor in the First Presidency, said this in his talk “Continue in Patience” from the April 2010 general conference (Priesthood Session).
Patience is a process of perfection.
The wait is doing work in us.

**The Spirit rides along.** We do not have to find patience on our own. When we are worn out and tempted to snap at the person next to us, the Spirit can help. Patience is something He grows in us as we ask.
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith,
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, Second Counselor in the First Presidency, said this in his talk “Continue in Patience” from the April 2010 general conference (Priesthood Session).
Patience is truly a fruit of the Spirit.
We can ask for it.
**Trust grows on long roads.** After many miles, a driver learns to trust the map. Each time we wait on the Lord and see Him come through, our trust grows deeper. Patience makes our faith stronger.
Then, my brethren, ye shall reap the rewards of your faith, and your diligence, and patience, and long-suffering, waiting for the tree to bring forth fruit unto you.
Elder Jeremy R. Jaggi of the Seventy said this in his talk “Let Patience Have Her Perfect Work, and Count It All Joy!” from the October 2020 general conference (Sunday Afternoon Session).
When we exercise patience, our faith increases.
Each mile adds to our trust.
**Arrival brings joy.** The family gets out of the car, stretches and laughs. The long trip is worth it. Those who patiently endure find the promise on the other side. Joy comes with it.
And so, after he had patiently endured, he obtained the promise.
Elder Jeremy R. Jaggi of the Seventy said this in his talk “Let Patience Have Her Perfect Work, and Count It All Joy!” from the October 2020 general conference (Sunday Afternoon Session).
As our faith increases, so does our joy.
The journey ends in joy.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when they had to be patient for something they wanted. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Jacob Serves Seven Years for Rachel

blocks.text: Jacob loved Rachel and was willing to work for her. The years were long. But love made the waiting lighter.
And Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her.
The wait was real, but love changed how it felt.

application.text: First, name one thing you are impatient about right now. Write down one small action you can take on it today.
Second, pick a way to travel well while you wait. It might be gratitude, a kind word or a short prayer.
Third, ask the Spirit to help you be patient this week. If the road feels too long, speak with your bishop or branch president.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that patience is a gift from God. I know that He walks with us on the long roads. I have seen how waiting can make us stronger and kinder. I know that Jesus Christ keeps His promises to those who endure. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

opening.text: A jigsaw puzzle with a thousand pieces looks impossible at first. The box shows a lovely picture. The table shows a mess. But a patient person starts with the edges, finds a few matching colors and slowly the picture grows. No one finishes a puzzle by wishing.
Patience works like that. Let us see what the scriptures and our leaders teach about building something one piece at a time.

mainMessage.text: The picture God has in mind for our lives comes together slowly. Patience is the steady work of placing one piece at a time and trusting the whole will come together.

blocks.text: **Placing pieces is active work.** A puzzle does not finish itself while we sit by. We pick up a piece, turn it and try it. Patience is not passive. We keep doing the next right thing while we wait for the bigger picture.

Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain. Be ye also patient; stablish your hearts: for the coming of the Lord draweth nigh.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, Second Counselor in the First Presidency, said this in his talk “Continue in Patience” from the April 2010 general conference (Priesthood Session).
Patience means active waiting and enduring.
We keep placing pieces.
**Finish well, not fast.** Rushing a puzzle means forcing pieces that do not fit. It is better to be steady. The Lord wants us to endure in a good spirit, not to grit our teeth and complain.
But that ye have patience, and bear with those afflictions, with a firm hope that ye shall one day rest from all your afflictions.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, Second Counselor in the First Presidency, said this in his talk “Continue in Patience” from the April 2010 general conference (Priesthood Session).
Patience is not simply enduring; it is enduring well!
A calm, hopeful spirit is part of the work.

**The picture builds piece by piece.** Early on, the pieces seem unrelated. Later, they begin to connect. Our lives work this way. Patience lets the pieces gather into something whole, and it changes us as we go.
And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope:
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, Second Counselor in the First Presidency, said this in his talk “Continue in Patience” from the April 2010 general conference (Priesthood Session).
Patience is a process of perfection.
The slow work is shaping us.
**A steady hand comes from the Spirit.** When we are tired of the puzzle, a quiet calm can help us sit down again. That calm is a gift. We can ask the Spirit for it.
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith,
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, Second Counselor in the First Presidency, said this in his talk “Continue in Patience” from the April 2010 general conference (Priesthood Session).
Patience is truly a fruit of the Spirit.
He can give us a steady hand.
**Faith grows with each piece.** Every time a piece fits, we trust the picture a bit more. Every time we wait on the Lord and see Him help, we trust Him more. Patience feeds our faith.
Then, my brethren, ye shall reap the rewards of your faith, and your diligence, and patience, and long-suffering, waiting for the tree to bring forth fruit unto you.
Elder Jeremy R. Jaggi of the Seventy said this in his talk “Let Patience Have Her Perfect Work, and Count It All Joy!” from the October 2020 general conference (Sunday Afternoon Session).
When we exercise patience, our faith increases.
Each piece builds trust.
**Joy when the last piece fits.** There is a quiet joy when the puzzle is done. In the same way, those who endure patiently find the promise at last. And the joy is deeper because of the wait.
And so, after he had patiently endured, he obtained the promise.
Elder Jeremy R. Jaggi of the Seventy said this in his talk “Let Patience Have Her Perfect Work, and Count It All Joy!” from the October 2020 general conference (Sunday Afternoon Session).
As our faith increases, so does our joy.
The final piece brings joy.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when patience brought them through something hard. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Job Stays Faithful and Is Blessed

blocks.text: Job lost nearly everything. Even then, he did not turn against God. After the hard season, the Lord blessed him again.

And said, Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return thither: the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord. In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly. And the Lord turned the captivity of Job, when he prayed for his friends: also the Lord gave Job twice as much as he had before.
Job kept his trust through a long, painful stretch. The Lord was faithful to him in the end.

application.text: First, think of one “puzzle” in your life that is taking longer than you hoped. Take one small step on it today.
Second, let go of the need to finish it fast. Choose to work on it with a calm heart.
Third, ask the Spirit for a steady hand each morning. If the work feels overwhelming, speak with your bishop or branch president.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that God is building something good in my life, one piece at a time. I know that patience is part of how He shapes us. I have felt my faith grow while I waited on Him. I know that Jesus Christ is faithful to the end. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

opening.text: A brick wall is not built in a day. A mason lays one brick, spreads a little mortar and lays another. At the end of the first day, the wall barely reaches the knees. But the mason comes back the next morning and does it again. Months later, there is a house.
Patience is the mason’s habit. Let us look at what it means to build slowly and well.

mainMessage.text: Good things are built a brick at a time. Patience keeps us coming back each day. The Lord is the builder, and He is pleased with steady work.

blocks.text: **One brick today.** A mason does not stand and stare at an empty lot. The mason lays a brick. We do not have to see the whole house. We only need to do today’s work, and keep doing it.

Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain. Be ye also patient; stablish your hearts: for the coming of the Lord draweth nigh.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, Second Counselor in the First Presidency, said this in his talk “Continue in Patience” from the April 2010 general conference (Priesthood Session).
Patience means active waiting and enduring.
We lay today’s brick.
**Build it well.** A wall that goes up in a rush may lean. A good mason takes care with each course. The same is true for us. The Lord wants us to hold steady and keep a good spirit while we build.
But that ye have patience, and bear with those afflictions, with a firm hope that ye shall one day rest from all your afflictions.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, Second Counselor in the First Presidency, said this in his talk “Continue in Patience” from the April 2010 general conference (Priesthood Session).
Patience is not simply enduring; it is enduring well!
Quality matters more than speed.

**The builder is being built.** A mason’s hands grow strong and sure over the years. The work shapes the worker. Patience shapes us too. It is not only about getting the house finished. It is about who we become on the way.
And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope:
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, Second Counselor in the First Presidency, said this in his talk “Continue in Patience” from the April 2010 general conference (Priesthood Session).
Patience is a process of perfection.
The work builds the worker.

**Strength we do not make ourselves.** When the work is hard and the sun is hot, a mason needs more than willpower. We need help beyond our own. The Spirit can give us the calm and strength to keep going.
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith,
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, Second Counselor in the First Presidency, said this in his talk “Continue in Patience” from the April 2010 general conference (Priesthood Session).
Patience is truly a fruit of the Spirit.
He can give us what we lack.
**Faith is the mortar.** Mortar holds the bricks together. Faith holds our patience together. And when we are patient, our faith grows firmer. They strengthen each other.
Then, my brethren, ye shall reap the rewards of your faith, and your diligence, and patience, and long-suffering, waiting for the tree to bring forth fruit unto you.
Elder Jeremy R. Jaggi of the Seventy said this in his talk “Let Patience Have Her Perfect Work, and Count It All Joy!” from the October 2020 general conference (Sunday Afternoon Session).
When we exercise patience, our faith increases.
Patience and faith hold each other up.
**Joy at the door.** One day the mason steps back and the house is finished. Someone walks in and is glad. Patient work ends in joy. And the promise comes to those who have endured.
And so, after he had patiently endured, he obtained the promise.
Elder Jeremy R. Jaggi of the Seventy said this in his talk “Let Patience Have Her Perfect Work, and Count It All Joy!” from the October 2020 general conference (Sunday Afternoon Session).
As our faith increases, so does our joy.
The finished work brings joy.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when steady, patient work paid off. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Noah Does as God Commanded

blocks.text: Noah did what God commanded. He kept building when the work was long and others did not understand. When the ark was ready, the Lord told him to come in.
Thus did Noah; according to all that God commanded him, so did he. And the Lord said unto Noah, Come thou and all thy house into the ark; for thee have I seen righteous before me in this generation.
Noah kept at the work, and the Lord was faithful to him.

application.text: First, pick one task you have been putting off because it feels too big. Do the first small piece today.
Second, set a simple daily habit you can keep for the next month. Let it be small enough to do even on a hard day.
Third, ask the Lord to bless your effort. If you feel discouraged, speak with your bishop or branch president.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that the Lord blesses steady effort. I know that patience is part of how He builds us. I have seen small daily acts turn into something lasting. I know that Jesus Christ is the master builder of our lives. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

opening.text: Someone knits a scarf. At first the work is a few rows of yarn on two needles. It does not look like much. After many evenings, a scarf takes shape. It is warm, and it was made one loop at a time. A knitter who tries to hurry will drop stitches. The calm, steady knitter finishes.
Patience has that quiet rhythm. Let us see what the Lord teaches about it.

mainMessage.text: Patience is a quiet, steady strength. It does not rush, and it does not quit. The Lord helps those who keep going one stitch at a time.

blocks.text: **One stitch after another.** A knitter does not sit and wait for the scarf to appear. The knitter works every row. Patience is active. We keep doing our part while the Lord does His.

Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain. Be ye also patient; stablish your hearts: for the coming of the Lord draweth nigh.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, Second Counselor in the First Presidency, said this in his talk “Continue in Patience” from the April 2010 general conference (Priesthood Session).
Patience means active waiting and enduring.
We keep knitting.
**Calm hands make good work.** A tense, hurried knitter makes mistakes. A calm one makes a smooth scarf. How we endure matters. A patient heart can hold steady even when things move slowly.
But that ye have patience, and bear with those afflictions, with a firm hope that ye shall one day rest from all your afflictions.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, Second Counselor in the First Presidency, said this in his talk “Continue in Patience” from the April 2010 general conference (Priesthood Session).
Patience is not simply enduring; it is enduring well!
A calm heart keeps the stitches even.

**We are being shaped too.** A knitter learns more with every row. The hands get quicker and the stitches get smoother. Patience is a process. It does something good in us while it works on the project.
And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope:
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, Second Counselor in the First Presidency, said this in his talk “Continue in Patience” from the April 2010 general conference (Priesthood Session).
Patience is a process of perfection.
The slow work is growing us.
**A gift we can ask for.** Some days a knitter feels worn out and wants to put the needles down. A gentle strength can come from outside ourselves. The Spirit can grow patience in us when we ask.
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith,
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, Second Counselor in the First Presidency, said this in his talk “Continue in Patience” from the April 2010 general conference (Priesthood Session).
Patience is truly a fruit of the Spirit.
We can ask for that fruit.
**Faith is the yarn.** The yarn runs through every stitch. Faith runs through everything we do while we wait. And each patient row makes the yarn stronger. Patience increases our faith.
Then, my brethren, ye shall reap the rewards of your faith, and your diligence, and patience, and long-suffering, waiting for the tree to bring forth fruit unto you.
Elder Jeremy R. Jaggi of the Seventy said this in his talk “Let Patience Have Her Perfect Work, and Count It All Joy!” from the October 2020 general conference (Sunday Afternoon Session).
When we exercise patience, our faith increases.
The thread grows stronger.
**Warm joy at the end.** When the scarf is finished, someone wears it, and it keeps them warm. Patient work leads to a gift. Those who endure patiently receive the promise, and joy follows.
And so, after he had patiently endured, he obtained the promise.
Elder Jeremy R. Jaggi of the Seventy said this in his talk “Let Patience Have Her Perfect Work, and Count It All Joy!” from the October 2020 general conference (Sunday Afternoon Session).
As our faith increases, so does our joy.
The finished work is a gift.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when patience helped them keep going. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: The Sons of Mosiah Bear Their Afflictions with Patience

blocks.text: Ammon and his brethren served among the Lamanites for years. At times they felt discouraged and wanted to turn back. The Lord comforted them and told them to be patient.

Now when our hearts were depressed, and we were about to turn back, behold, the Lord comforted us, and said: Go amongst thy brethren, the Lamanites, and bear with patience thine afflictions, and I will give you success. And now behold, we have come, and been forth amongst them; and we have been patient in our sufferings, and we have suffered every privation; yea, we have traveled from house to house, relying upon the mercies of the world—not upon the mercies of the world alone but upon the mercies of God.
They kept going, one house at a time. The Lord kept His promise of success.

application.text: First, choose one thing in your life that needs slow, steady care. Spend ten quiet minutes on it today.
Second, when you feel like putting it down, say a short prayer for patience first.
Third, notice one small sign of progress this week and thank God for it. If you need help carrying a heavy burden, speak with your bishop or branch president.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that patience is a quiet strength from God. I know that He helps us keep going when we are tired. I have seen slow, steady effort bring lasting good. I know that Jesus Christ is patient with us. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

opening.text: The Grand Canyon was not dug in a season. A river carved it, drop by drop and year by year. The water is soft. The rock is hard. But the river keeps flowing, and over a very long time, the rock gives way.
Patience has that kind of quiet power. Let us see how it works in our lives.

mainMessage.text: Steady, gentle effort can do what force cannot. Patience does not rush or quit. It keeps flowing, and the Lord shapes something good along the way.

blocks.text: **The river keeps flowing.** A river does not stop and wait for the canyon to appear. It moves every day. Patience is active in the same way. We keep moving, doing what is ours to do, while the work takes its time.

Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain. Be ye also patient; stablish your hearts: for the coming of the Lord draweth nigh.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, Second Counselor in the First Presidency, said this in his talk “Continue in Patience” from the April 2010 general conference (Priesthood Session).
Patience means active waiting and enduring.
We keep flowing.
**Gentle, not forced.** A river does not roar at the rock. It flows with a steady calm. Enduring well is like that. We can hold on without bitterness, and keep a soft heart while the work is slow.
But that ye have patience, and bear with those afflictions, with a firm hope that ye shall one day rest from all your afflictions.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, Second Counselor in the First Presidency, said this in his talk “Continue in Patience” from the April 2010 general conference (Priesthood Session).
Patience is not simply enduring; it is enduring well!
Gentleness is part of strength.
**The shape comes over time.** A canyon takes its form slowly. Our character does too. Patience is part of how God shapes us. Each hard day adds a little to who we become.
And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope:
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, Second Counselor in the First Presidency, said this in his talk “Continue in Patience” from the April 2010 general conference (Priesthood Session).
Patience is a process of perfection.
Time does its quiet work.
**A river is fed from above.** A river does not make its own water. Rain and snow send it down from the heights. Patience is also something we receive. The Spirit can pour it into us when we ask.
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith,
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf, Second Counselor in the First Presidency, said this in his talk “Continue in Patience” from the April 2010 general conference (Priesthood Session).
Patience is truly a fruit of the Spirit.
It flows to us from above.
**Faith deepens the channel.** As the river flows, its channel gets deeper. As we wait with patience, our faith gets deeper too. We learn that God can be trusted, and that makes the next wait easier.
Then, my brethren, ye shall reap the rewards of your faith, and your diligence, and patience, and long-suffering, waiting for the tree to bring forth fruit unto you.
Elder Jeremy R. Jaggi of the Seventy said this in his talk “Let Patience Have Her Perfect Work, and Count It All Joy!” from the October 2020 general conference (Sunday Afternoon Session).
When we exercise patience, our faith increases.
Each wait deepens our trust.
**The view is worth it.** Visitors stand at the rim of a canyon and gasp. Something beautiful came from a long, patient process. Those who endure patiently obtain the promise, and joy comes with it.
And so, after he had patiently endured, he obtained the promise.
Elder Jeremy R. Jaggi of the Seventy said this in his talk “Let Patience Have Her Perfect Work, and Count It All Joy!” from the October 2020 general conference (Sunday Afternoon Session).
As our faith increases, so does our joy.
The long work ends in wonder.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when patience led to something lasting. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Nephi Builds the Ship Step by Step

blocks.text: Nephi was told to build a ship. He had never built one. He did not rush or build it his own way. He worked the timbers as the Lord showed him, step by step.

And it came to pass that they did worship the Lord, and did go forth with me; and we did work timbers of curious workmanship. And the Lord did show me from time to time after what manner I should work the timbers of the ship. Now I, Nephi, did not work the timbers after the manner which was learned by men, neither did I build the ship after the manner of men; but I did build it after the manner which the Lord had shown unto me; wherefore, it was not after the manner of men.
The Lord showed Nephi “from time to time.” Nephi was patient enough to follow one step at a time.

application.text: First, name one slow change you are hoping to see in your life. Tell the Lord you will keep working on it.
Second, choose one gentle habit to practice daily. Let it be small and steady.
Third, ask the Spirit for patience each morning. If you need guidance, speak with your bishop or branch president.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that God shapes us slowly and with love. I know that patience is a gift of the Spirit. I have felt my faith deepen as I waited on the Lord. I know that Jesus Christ is patient with us, and that He keeps His promises. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.
